target_customer: Urban riders in Latin American cities paying per ride for shared electric scooters
problem: Short urban trips in congested Latin American cities lacked cheap clean transport; Grin placed dockless electric scooters in Mexico City from 2018.
business_model: Usage-based scooter sharing with per-minute pricing, later a subscription and wallet

founders.name: Sergio Romo
founders.background_notes: Later became an angel investor per YC page.

founders.name: Jonathan Lewy
founders.background_notes: Named as Grin co-founder by TechCrunch 2019.

competitors.name: Lime
competitors.what: US dockless scooter and bike sharing

technical_complexity.rationale: Scooters were off the shelf hardware with an app and fleet operations; the hard part was operations and local compliance.

defensibility.rationale: Scooter sharing had no switching costs; Bird and Lime had far more capital.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Grin merged with Yellow in January 2019 to form Grow Mobility; Lime and others also retreated from Latin America.

market_need_then: Mexico City traffic and pollution plus the 2018 global scooter boom created demand; the city revoked Grin's permit in February 2019 per a later report.

identity.visual_style: Green scooters referred to as Grin's green scooters

brand_strength.rationale: No source explains the name or shows brand pull; the green scooters were recognizable but the brand was absorbed into Grow Mobility.

pivots.why: Grow merged with Flinto; Lewy called the wallet the future of the company

outcome_analysis: Grin launched in 2018, raised a $45.7M Series A in October 2018, merged with Yellow in January 2019 into Grow Mobility and reportedly raised $150M, then added Flinto. By January 2020 it was retreating from 14 Brazilian cities, laying off a reported 600 and facing unpaid staff reports, with used scooters sold off. Permit problems in Mexico City and thin scooter economics are consistent with sources but no company post-mortem exists.
notes: ongrin.com returned 404.
